4.1.l: Pediatric Hip — Pelvic Osteotomies & Late Acetabular Dysplasia
4.1.b:
A pelvic osteotomy fixes the socket; it is chosen by the hip, the symptoms and the child's maturity.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "when do you do a pelvic osteotomy?"
- "With **open reduction**, or for **residual** or **late** dysplasia."
- "Only in a **symptomatic** hip that is **concentrically reduced**."
- "Do not operate to treat an X-ray."

### Four Indications
The lecture groups the patients into four situations.
- Combined with open reduction in the walking child → 03 DDH Treatment
- **Residual dysplasia** after any treatment: index not improving or subluxation
- **Late-presenting dysplasia** in a hip once treated and doing well
- **Primary dysplasia** first seen in adolescence, never treated

#### The Typical Adolescent
- Acetabular index above **40°** in a severe case
[[FIG: Fig 4.1 · 4.1
- Centre-edge angle reversed: below zero
- Mature or immature: the triradiate cartilage changes the choice

### Symptoms Decide
A dysplastic film alone is not an indication.
- Symptomatic hip → treatment is required
- Asymptomatic dysplasia → much debated; finding it does not oblige surgery
- Judge the indication and the result by **function**, not by the film

PITFALL — "the film is bad, operate?"
- A textbook-ugly film in a child who walks well tempts the surgeon.
- Say → "I operate for pain, limp or abductor fatigue, not for an X-ray."

### Radiological Indications
Two angles carry the decision
[[FIG: Fig 4.2 · 4.1
- Centre-edge angle (CE) under **20°**
- Acetabular index over **15–20°** (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Lateral CE 20–25° = borderline dysplasia (Campbell)
- Untreated lateral CE under 16° → arthritis by age 65 (Campbell)

### Prerequisites
A reconstructive osteotomy needs a hip that can sit in the socket.
- The head is **concentrically reduced**, or reduced at the same sitting
- The joint is congruent: checked on the abduction–internal rotation view
- A reasonably spherical head and a good range of motion
- No congruence possible → a salvage procedure, never a reconstruction

MEMORY HOOK — the house and the key
- A new roof is useless if the tenant is outside: reduce the head first, then build the roof.

4.2.l: Pediatric Hip — Pelvic Osteotomies & Late Acetabular Dysplasia
4.2.b:
Late dysplasia presents with complaints the infant never had.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how does adolescent dysplasia present?"
- "**Pain and fatigue** on walking: abductors work too hard."
- "Groin pain on standing or running: **labral shear**."
- "Limp: **Trendelenburg**, or waddling if bilateral."

### Symptoms
Each complaint has a mechanism.
- Unstable fulcrum → excessive muscle force → fatigue → pain
- Shear on the **labrum** and capsule → pain on prolonged standing
- Labral impingement → pain sitting, in forced flexion and adduction
- Symptoms usually start between the second and fifth decades

### Gait
The short abductor lever shows in the walk
[[FIG: Fig 4.3 · 4.2
- Abductor insufficiency → **Trendelenburg** gait
- Bilateral → waddling gait
- Positive impingement (FADIR) test in labral damage
- FADIR = flexion, adduction, internal rotation

4.3.l: Pediatric Hip — Pelvic Osteotomies & Late Acetabular Dysplasia
4.3.b:
One film is never enough; late dysplasia needs an array of views.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "which films before a pelvic osteotomy?"
- "AP supine and **standing**; frog lateral for the head."
- "**Abduction–internal rotation** view: is it congruent?"
- "**False profile** for anterior cover; 3D CT for shape."

### The Imaging Array
Each view answers one question.

| View | Question answered |
|---|---|
| AP supine | Shenton line, acetabular index, CE angle |
| AP standing | does the hip sublux on standing? |
| Frog lateral | is the head round? |
| Abduction–internal rotation | congruent and reducible, or fixed? |
| False profile | anterior cover: anterior CE angle |
| 3D CT | head and socket shape; head subtraction |

### Anteroposterior View
The supine AP film carries the three classic signs.
- **Shenton line**: neck to superior pubic ramus, one smooth arc
[[FIG: Fig 4.4 · 4.3
- Broken line → subluxated or dislocated hip
- Acetabular index from Hilgenreiner's line through both triradiate cartilages
[[FIG: Fig 4.5 · 4.3
- Normal index: under 20° in young children, under 15° older (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- CE angle: vertical through the head centre, line to the acetabular edge
[[FIG: Fig 4.6 · 4.3
- Lateral CE normal 25–39°; under 20° dysplastic (Orthobullets)
- Tönnis (sourcil) angle over 10° = dysplasia (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 4.7 · 4.3

#### In the Adult-Sized Hip
- Severe dysplasia breaks Shenton line: the head rides up
[[FIG: Fig 4.8 · 4.3
- Look for a lateral hip centre and a broad teardrop
- Cam morphology coexists in 10–40% of dysplastic hips (Campbell)

### Standing View
Weight bearing unmasks instability
[[FIG: Fig 4.9 · 4.3
- Supine: head close to the teardrop
- Standing: the distance grows → **subluxation on standing**
[[FIG: Fig 4.10 · 4.3
- This hip has high shear and a Trendelenburg gait

### Frog Lateral View
The frog film studies the head, not the socket
[[FIG: Fig 4.11 · 4.3
- Like a prisoner's photographs: front and side of the same head
- Equal diameters on AP and frog → **round head**
- Unequal → flattened head: a redirection may make it incongruent

### Abduction–Internal Rotation View
This film predicts the hip after the osteotomy
[[FIG: Fig 4.12 · 4.3
- Head descends into the socket → reducible: reconstruction possible
- Shenton line restored → spherical congruent hip
[[FIG: Fig 4.13 · 4.3
- Head stays out → fixed subluxation: think salvage
- Campbell uses slight flexion and abduction to mimic a periacetabular osteotomy
[[FIG: Fig 4.14 · 4.3

#### The Anteversion Trap
- A hip may look subluxated on a film in external rotation
[[FIG: Fig 4.15 · 4.3
- The lesser trochanter is prominent; the neck is seen end-on
- In internal rotation the head sits in the socket: only **anteversion**

PITFALL — "subluxed on the AP, so osteotomy?"
- The lecturer warned three times: an externally rotated film fakes subluxation.
- Say → "Repeat in internal rotation before calling it subluxation."

### False Profile View
The AP shows lateral cover; the false profile shows anterior cover
[[FIG: Fig 4.16 · 4.3
- Patient standing, pelvis turned about **65°** to the film (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- The opposite leg steps back; the affected hip stays against the film
- Anterior CE angle: vertical from the head centre to the anterior edge
[[FIG: Fig 4.17 · 4.3
- Normal 25–40°; under 20° = poor anterior cover (Orthobullets)
[[FIG: Fig 4.18 · 4.3
- Poor anterior cover → plan anterior rotation
- Ask the radiographer by name of the view; few centres know it

### Three-Dimensional CT
3D CT is one of the most useful studies today
[[FIG: Fig 4.19 · 4.3
- Shows the shape of the head and of the acetabulum
- **Head subtraction** shows the bare socket from outside
- Campbell adds low-dose CT for acetabular and femoral version

### Aim of the Osteotomy
Compare the films before and after; four lines should change
[[FIG: Fig 4.20 · 4.3
- Concentric head in the socket
- Shenton line restored
- CE angle increased; acetabular index decreased
- Good cover of the head: a normal-looking hip

MEMORY HOOK — the prisoner's photographs
- The frog lateral is the mugshot from the side: one face in two poses, and it must match to be round.

4.4.l: Pediatric Hip — Pelvic Osteotomies & Late Acetabular Dysplasia
4.4.b:
Name the osteotomy by what it does, not by who described it.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you classify pelvic osteotomies?"
- "**Reconstructive** (congruent hip) or **salvage** (incongruent hip)."
- "Reconstructive = **redirectional** or **reshaping**."
- "Salvage = **Chiari** and **shelf**."

### Reconstructive Versus Salvage
Congruity, not the name, decides the class
[[FIG: Fig 4.21 · 4.4

| | Reconstructive | Salvage |
|---|---|---|
| Hip | congruent when reduced | incongruent, damaged |
| Aim | restore normal morphology | halt damage, keep function |
| Cover by | articular cartilage | capsule → fibrocartilage |
| Examples | Salter, Pemberton, Dega, triple, Ganz | Chiari, shelf |

- The Handbook links them to age: reconstructive under 8 years, salvage over 8
- A Ganz done on an incongruent hip is still a salvage

### Redirectional Versus Reshaping
Each mainly fixes one defect; neither is pure.

| | Redirectional | Reshaping (acetabuloplasty) |
|---|---|---|
| Defect | wrong direction, normal depth | shallow socket, high index |
| Mechanism | rotates the whole acetabulum | folds the roof down |
| Volume | unchanged | reduced |
| Examples | Salter, triple, Ganz | Pemberton, Dega, San Diego |

### Basic Principles
Four rules shape every cut.
- The head stays **inside** the socket while the osteotomy is opened
- The head is the mould; the roof is the dough
- Cuts never cross an **open triradiate cartilage**
- Closer to the acetabulum → more reshaping; farther → more redirection

### What Holds the Fragment
Mobility depends on what still tethers the acetabulum
[[FIG: Fig 4.22 · 4.4
- Symphysis pubis, **sacrospinous** and **sacrotuberous** ligaments hold it
[[FIG: Fig 4.23 · 4.4
- Salter, Pemberton, Dega: all three still hold it
- Triple with an ischial cut near the joint: sacrospinous only
[[FIG: Fig 4.24 · 4.4
- Ganz and Bernese-type triple: completely free

MEMORY HOOK — three ropes
- The acetabulum is a boat tied by three ropes: the symphysis, the sacrospinous, the sacrotuberous. Each cut you add unties one more.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how does the Salter osteotomy work?"
- "Complete iliac cut from the **sciatic notch** to above the **AIIS**."
- "Fragment hinges on the **symphysis pubis**; wedge graft and wires."
- "Age **18 months–6 years**; congruent hip; mild dysplasia."

### Salter Innominate Osteotomy
Salter saw that the dysplastic acetabulum faces anterolaterally, so he turned it.

#### Technique
- Anterior approach; release adductors and iliopsoas tendon
[[FIG: Fig 4.25 · 4.5
- Gigli saw from the sciatic notch to just above the AIIS
- Figure-of-four position opens the cut
[[FIG: Fig 4.26 · 4.5
- Fragment shifted anteriorly, inferiorly and laterally; closed posteriorly
- Full-thickness iliac crest wedge; one or two K-wires
[[FIG: Fig 4.27 · 4.5
- Never pull the proximal fragment upward: it subluxes the sacroiliac joint
[[FIG: Fig 4.28 · 4.5

#### Indications and Limits
- Child **18 months to 6 years** (Campbell); best results under 8
- Congruent hip; acetabular index needs under 10–15° of correction
- Contraindicated in nonconcentric hips and severe dysplasia
- Spica 6–8 weeks, then wires removed
- May lengthen the leg up to 1 cm (Miller)
- Handbook: unilateral only and weak after 3–4 years; Campbell uses it to 6
- Before and after a Salter osteotomy
[[FIG: Fig 4.29 · 4.5

#### Disadvantages
- Correction is limited: the symphysis is a stiff hinge
- Metal fixation and a second operation to remove it
- Axis of rotation is unknown: all tethers steer it
- The lecturer sees falling use; bladder exstrophy closure still needs pelvic osteotomy

PITFALL — Salter and the posterior wall
- The lecture says Salter adds retroversion; Campbell says it does not, but it does move cover forward.
- Say → "Salter brings cover anterolaterally; avoid it when the posterior wall is deficient."

#### Structures at Risk
- Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve in the approach
- Sciatic nerve at the notch: strict subperiosteal retractors
- Obturator nerve medially; femoral nerve under the iliopsoas

### Double Innominate Osteotomy (Sutherland)
A second cut was added to free the hinge
[[FIG: Fig 4.30 · 4.5
- Salter cut + pubic cut lateral and parallel to the symphysis
- The pubic cut is far from the joint → large displacement for little rotation
- Off-ending and non-union → abandoned

### Triple Innominate Osteotomy
Three cuts around the acetabulum free it from the symphysis
[[FIG: Fig 4.31 · 4.5
- Ilium (as Salter), superior pubic ramus and ischium
- Types: **Steel**, **Tönnis**, Le Coeur (Handbook)
- Graft and pins hold the fragment
[[FIG: Fig 4.32 · 4.5

#### Level of the Ischial Cut
The ischial cut decides how free the fragment is.

| Ischial cut | Still tethered by | Mobility |
|---|---|---|
| Ischiopubic ramus, far (Steel) | sacrospinous + sacrotuberous | limited |
| Ischium near the joint (Tönnis) | sacrospinous only | high |
| Proximal to the ischial spine (Bernese) | nothing | free |

#### Steel Technique and Care
- Posterior incision for the ischium, anterior for pubis and ilium
- Spica 8–12 weeks; union usually by **12 weeks** (Campbell)
- Avoid excess external rotation of the fragment: nonunion and lost posterior cover
- Pelvic distortion may prevent natural childbirth later
- Used less since the periacetabular osteotomy

### Bernese-Type Triple Pelvic Osteotomy
This is the Ganz cut finished into the sciatic notch
[[FIG: Fig 4.33 · 4.5
- Pubic and ischial cuts as in Ganz
- Iliac cut carried to the **sciatic notch** instead of the posterior column
[[FIG: Fig 4.34 · 4.5
- Same free fragment as Ganz, but safe with an **open triradiate cartilage** (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Demanding surgery: experienced hands only

#### Lecture Case: Large Head
- Obvious dysplasia with a **large head** on AP and frog films
[[FIG: Fig 4.35 · 4.5
- Dega would shrink the socket → mismatch with the big head
- False profile: anterior cover respectable, lateral cover poor
[[FIG: Fig 4.36 · 4.5
- 3D CT confirms the uncovered head
[[FIG: Fig 4.37 · 4.5
- Triple osteotomy: rotate the socket around the head
[[FIG: Fig 4.38 · 4.5
- After: full cover on the AP and the false profile
[[FIG: Fig 4.39 · 4.5

### Rotational Acetabular Osteotomies
Wagner, Tönnis spherical and Eppright (dial) cuts are historical
[[FIG: Fig 4.40 · 4.5
- Limited correction in the adult
- Impaired perfusion of the fragment → non-union
- Replaced by the Ganz periacetabular osteotomy

MEMORY HOOK — the pen
- Turn a pen by its tip and you swing the whole arm; turn it near the middle and a flick will do. Cuts close to the socket rotate it cheaply.

Salvage halts damage; it never restores a normal hip.

- Early osteoarthritis where reconstruction is impossible
- Older child: over 6–8 years (Handbook); Chiari rarely under 10 (Campbell)
- Other salvage: fusion, resection, arthroplasty in adolescence

- Proximal fragment becomes the roof; capsule interposed

Age, triradiate cartilage, congruity and head size pick the operation.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "which osteotomy for which child?"
- "Under 8, congruent: **Salter, Pemberton or Dega**."
- "Older, open triradiate: **triple**; closed: **Ganz**."
- "Incongruent at any age: **Chiari or shelf**."

### By Age and Triradiate Cartilage
Campbell's table is the exam answer (Campbell).

| Osteotomy | Age | Key indication |
|---|---|---|
| Salter | 18 months–6 years | congruent; index correction under 10–15° |
| Pemberton | 18 months–10 years | correction over 10–15°; small head, big socket |
| Steel triple | late childhood, open triradiate | residual dysplasia, symptoms, congruent |
| Ganz | closed triradiate | same, mature pelvis |
| Chiari or shelf | usually older children | incongruent, symptoms, nothing else possible |

- Miller over 8 years: open plate → triple, double or Staheli
- Closed plate → Ganz or Chiari

### Five Questions on the Film
Answer them in order before naming a cut.
- Is the head congruent in abduction–internal rotation? No → salvage
- Is the triradiate cartilage open? Yes → no Ganz
- Is the defect depth or direction? Depth → reshape; direction → redirect
- Is the head large? Yes → redirect: reshaping shrinks the socket
- Is the deficiency posterior? Yes → Dega or San Diego, not Salter

PITFALL — "Salter for the cerebral palsy hip?"
- In cerebral palsy the deficiency is usually posterosuperior; Salter uncovers the back further.
- Say → "Dega or San Diego for the spastic hip."
